title_original: Killer frogs and rat-murdering fairies: the macabre cards Victorians sent at Christmas
excerpt_original: ‘Absurd and unexpectedly violent’ cards reproduced by English Heritage are a glimpse into darker, more subversive side of Victorian festivities Chestnuts roasting on an open fire. Rosy-cheeked children singing carols in the snow. And a dead rat suspended over a fire by a group…

blocks.text: C hestnuts roasting on an open fire. Rosy-cheeked children singing carols in the snow. And a dead rat suspended over a fire by a group of fairies wearing the skins of its murdered family. Merry Christmas to you!

The phrase “Victorian Christmas”, to many people, conjures up sentimental images of warmth and good will. But the Victorians themselves held a view of the festive period that could be much darker – and weirder.

A new set of genuine historic cards that have been reproduced for sale by English Heritage is a reminder of this macabre and darkly humorous view of the festivities, offering season’s greetings that are anything but cosy.

A robin – that cheerful figure of festivity – lies dead and cold on the ground, under the slogan: “A Joyous Christmas to You.” Another stands triumphantly on the breast of a turkey it has just murdered, knife and fork in hand, in an offbeat parody of the tale of George and the Dragon: “Cheerful Good Wishes – Always a knife and fork for you”, reads the motto.

Perhaps the oddest image of the set depicts a dead frog lying spreadeagled on the ground with a tiny dagger in its chest, while its fellow frog killer – for some reason wearing trousers and a waistcoat – escapes with a bag of loot. Nothing says “A Merry Christmas to you” like frog theft and murder.

Peter Moore, a curator of collections and interiors at English Heritage , said the twisted Christmas images emerged during the mid-19th century, when the seasonal card industry was expanding rapidly, driven by advances in print technology and the growth of the postal service.

blocks.alt: Victorian Christmas card illustration of a dead robin lying on its back beneath berry branches.
blocks.caption: One card reads ‘A Joyous Christmas to You’ and depicts a dead robin. Photograph: Mary Evans Picture Library/The David Pearson Collection

blocks.text: “As sending Christmas cards became increasingly popular, publishers competed for customers with unusual, eye-catching and sometimes downright bizarre designs,” he said. “Many of these illustrations play with the uncanny, depicting animals behaving like people in scenes that could be humorous, absurd or unexpectedly violent.”

They also echo the darker and more subversive traditions of the winter festival, said Moore. From the Roman festival of Saturnalia to the Welsh tradition of Mari Lwyd, where wassailers went door to door with a horse’s head, to the Catalan “caganer”, a figurine posed as if defecating that is placed in nativity scenes, “a lot of the alternative folklore traditions across Europe come from the idea of winter being dark and cold and threatening, a time to think about death and redemption,” Moore added.
Some of the imagery may have made more immediate sense to the Victorians than it does today, said Moore, with the dead robin as an intriguing example.

“Robins became associated with Christmas through their connection with Victorian postmen, whose red uniforms earned them the nickname ‘robins’,” he said. “Some historians have also suggested that the bird carried religious symbolism, with a popular Christian tradition holding that the robin’s red breast was stained with Christ’s blood as it sought to comfort him on the cross.”

blocks.alt: Christmas card showing fur-clad figures roasting an animal over a fire in snow.
blocks.caption: Rat-murdering fairies would have been less alien in the Victorian era, when stories of elves and pixies were popular. Photograph: Mary Evans Picture Library/The David Pearson Collection

blocks.text: The rat-murdering fairies, too, while deeply odd today, would have been less alien in a culture in which stories of elves and pixies were wildly popular. That image is captioned, “With the compliments of the season” and, Moore said: “It’s so hard to say if there’s any kind of irony there. This is a visual culture and history that isn’t really recorded, so we’ll never really know how people responded. I’d love to be able to go back in time and ask people what they made of it.”

He had been unable, similarly, to find any fable or potential inspiration for the festive frog murder, but said it was probably intended as a pantomime-style scene. “The dagger is very theatrical, don’t you think? It has got the weird air of a froggy version of a Shakespearean tragedy.”
The limited edition cards are available – alongside more traditional festive cards – at English Heritage gift shops .
